introduction.p: Substitution follows from the chain rule. When x=g(u), the expression dx=g\prime(u)\,du records the factor that converts the integrand to the new variable:
The sign of g\prime records orientation. In a definite integral, the endpoints must also be expressed in the new variable.

subsection.title: dx as an oriented step
subsection.p: The definite integral
accumulates from a to b. The direction matters.
If a<b, we move left to right. A small step dx is positive.
If b<a, we move right to left. A small step dx is negative.
That is why
The symbol dx carries the direction of traversal.

subsection.p: The function f(x) supplies the density, rate, or height. The dx supplies the oriented step along the x-axis.
This is why units work naturally.
The dx is part of the meaning of the integral.

exercise.title: Why should f(x)\,dx be read as one unit?

statement.p: A Riemann sum is built from terms f(x_i^*)\Delta x_i. In your own words, why is f(x)\,dx the small signed amount being accumulated, and why do units such as grams per centimeter times centimeters confirm that reading?

hint.p: The function supplies a density, rate, or height. The factor dx supplies the oriented step along the axis. Together they make a small contribution of the accumulated quantity.

note.title: Moral
note.p: The definite integral records both size and direction. Applications decide whether that signed quantity is the desired physical quantity.

exercise.title: Why does substitution multiply by g'(u)?

statement.p: If x=g(u), then f(x)\,dx=f(g(u))g'(u)\,du. In your own words, why is this a change of measuring stick rather than a trick with symbols, and why must the limits change with the variable?

hint.p: Equal steps in u need not be equal steps in x. The factor g'(u) converts a du-step into the corresponding oriented dx-step, and the endpoints must be rewritten in the new coordinate.

note.title: Substitution rule, read geometrically
note.p: Let f be continuous on an interval J, and let g have a continuous derivative on the interval between \alpha and \beta, with all its values in J. When x=g(u),

To prove the rule, choose an antiderivative F of f, which exists by Part I. The chain rule gives (F\circ g)'(u)=f(g(u))g'(u). Part II makes the right-hand integral F(g(\beta))-F(g(\alpha))=F(b)-F(a), exactly the left-hand integral. No monotonicity of g is needed: oriented contributions cancel if it doubles back. The derivative g'(u) converts du-steps into oriented dx-steps.

subsection.p: The limits are part of the substitution. They are not decoration.

exercise.title: What does \int_a^b dF=F(b)-F(a) say in words?

statement.p: If dF=F'(x)\,dx, Part II becomes the compact statement that accumulating the small changes of F recovers final value minus initial value. In your own words, why is that the same theorem as integrating a derivative, and why does the boundary of an oriented interval appear as endpoint minus starting point?

hint.p: The small pieces dF are the instantaneous changes of F. Adding them along [a,b] should reconstruct the net change of F from a to b.
